title: Random Forest Variable Importance and SHAP on Pima Indians Diabetes (Python)
text:
This document shows how to compute Random Forest variable importance and SHAP values for the Pima Indians Diabetes dataset using Python.

Load the dataset.

section: 3. Train / test split and Random Forest model
text:
3. Train / test split and Random Forest model


Code
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=123, stratify=y
)

rf = RandomForestClassifier(
    n_estimators=300,
    max_depth=None,
    random_state=123,
    n_jobs=-1
)

rf.fit(X_train, y_train)

y_pred_proba = rf.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, y_pred_proba)
auc

title: Random Forest Variable Importance and SHAP on Pima Indians Diabetes (Python)
text:
4. Random Forest Variable Importance (impurity-based)
Here we use the standard feature_importances_ attribute from scikit-learn, which reflects the average decrease in Gini impurity contributed by each feature.


Code
importances = rf.feature_importances_
vip = pd.Series(importances, index=feature_names).sort_values(ascending=True)

plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
vip.plot(kind="barh")
plt.xlabel("Mean decrease in impurity")
plt.title("Random Forest Variable Importance (Pima Indians)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()











Code
result = permutation_importance(
rf,
X_test,
y_test,
n_repeats=20,
random_state=123,
scoring="roc_auc",
n_jobs=-1
)


perm_importance = pd.Series(
result.importances_mean,
index=feature_names
).sort_values(ascending=True)
display(perm_importance)
perm_importance.plot(kind="barh")
plt.xlabel("Mean decrease in ROC AUC\n(permuting each feature on test set)")
plt.title("Permutation Importance (Random Forest)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

text:
5. SHAP values with TreeExplainer
SHAP provides local (per‑instance) and global explanations. For tree models, TreeExplainer gives an efficient way to compute exact Shapley values.
This visualises how each feature for this patient pushes the prediction away from the baseline towards the final diabetes risk estimate.

You now have:

Random Forest VIP via feature_importances_.
SHAP‑based global importance and summary plots.
A template for local SHAP explanations on individual patients.

section: 7. Simple linear model: coefficients as a basic importance measure
text:
7. Simple linear model: coefficients as a basic importance measure
For comparison with Random Forest VIP and SHAP, we can also fit a simple linear model and look directly at the coefficients.
Here we use LogisticRegression (a linear model for binary outcomes).


Code
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

log_reg = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, solver="liblinear")

log_reg.fit(X_train, y_train)

coef = pd.Series(log_reg.coef_[0], index=feature_names).sort_values(ascending=True)
intercept = log_reg.intercept_[0]

print("Intercept (log-odds):", intercept)
coef

Positive coefficients mean that higher values of the feature increase the log-odds of diabetes,
negative coefficients mean they decrease the log-odds.
We can also visualise these coefficients:


Code
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
coef.plot(kind="barh")
plt.xlabel("Coefficient (log-odds scale)")
plt.title("Logistic Regression Coefficients (Pima Indians)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









This provides a very simple, fully interpretable baseline to compare with:

Logistic regression coefficients (linear, global, easy to interpret but may be too simplistic).
Random Forest VIP (nonlinear model, impurity-based importance).
SHAP values (local and global feature attributions consistent with the model’s behaviour).

Explainable AI
You are going to see the power of the DALEX package https://github.com/ModelOriented/DALEX, where the methods seen in class AND MORE, are encoded.
First, make sure you have the packages installed:

# Install required packages
#install.packages(c("tidymodels", "mlbench", "DALEX", "DALEXtra", "modelStudio"))

Now load them into our session:

library(tidymodels)

library(mlbench)
library(DALEX)
library(DALEXtra)
library(modelStudio)

Now we are going to fit a random forest model (black box) on our well known PimaIndiansDiabetes dataset. We want to predict diabetes, so we are building a classification predictive model.

# Load and prepare data
data("PimaIndiansDiabetes")

PimaIndiansDiabetes <- PimaIndiansDiabetes %>%
       mutate(diabetes = as.factor(ifelse(diabetes == "pos", 1, 0)))

Classic train test split:

set.seed(123)

data_split <- initial_split(PimaIndiansDiabetes, prop = 0.8)
train_data <- training(data_split)
test_data <- testing(data_split)

Pre-processing

# Define recipe and model
diabetes_recipe <- recipe(diabetes ~ ., data = train_data) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric()) 

Model fitting (no hyperparameter tuning here)

rf_model <- rand_forest(mtry = 3, trees = 500, min_n = 10) %>%
  set_engine("ranger") %>%
  set_mode("classification")

# Create and fit workflow
rf_workflow <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(diabetes_recipe) %>%
  add_model(rf_model)

rf_fit <- fit(rf_workflow, data = train_data)

Evaluate model on test set

rf_predictions <- predict(rf_fit, new_data = test_data, type = "prob") %>%
  bind_cols(predict(rf_fit, new_data = test_data)) %>%
  bind_cols(test_data)

metrics <- rf_predictions %>%
  metrics(truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class)

print(metrics)

title: Comparison of Break Down, LIME and Shapley values
text:
For a bit more insight, you can go through this tutorial obtained from here: https://github.com/ModelOriented/DALEX-docs/blob/master/vignettes/Comparison%20between%20breakdown%2C%20lime%2C%20shapley.Rmd Should take 2 mins to run.
In the vignette below we will see how methods implemented in DALEX R packages focuses on variables in selected model. For our model we consider Break Down, LIME and Shapley values.
library(DALEX)
library(lime)
library(randomForest)
crumbs: Comparison of Break Down, LIME and Shapley values

title: Comparison of Break Down, LIME and Shapley values
text:
Break Down
Break Down is the methodology delevoped by Przemysław Biecek and Mateusz Staniak. A description of the method can be found here.
This methodology is implemented by Przemysław Biecek and Mateusz Staniak in the R package breakDown. Currently available in the R package DALEX.
The breakDown package is a model agnostic tool for decomposition of predictions from black boxes. Break Down Table shows contributions of every variable to a final prediction. Break Down Profile presents variable contributions in a concise graphical way.
crumbs: Comparison of Break Down, LIME and Shapley values

title: Comparison of Break Down, LIME and Shapley values
text:
LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations)
LIME is the methodology developed by Marco Tulio Ribeiro, Sameer Singh, and Carlos Guestrin. A description of the method can be found here.
The purpose of LIME is to explain the predictions of black box classifiers. What this means is that for any given prediction and any given classifier it is able to determine a small set of features in the original data that has driven the outcome of the prediction. Using here package lime is an R port of the Python lime package (https://github.com/marcotcr/lime) developed by the authors of the lime approach for black-box model explanations.
crumbs: Comparison of Break Down, LIME and Shapley values

title: Comparison of Break Down, LIME and Shapley values
text:
Shapley value
A methodology based on the use of Shapley value known from game theory to explain predictions is developed by Scott Lundberg and Su-In Lee. A description of the method can be found here.
The Shapley value is a method that gives a solution to the following problem: A coalition of players play a game, for which they get a payout, but it is not clear how to distribute the payout fairly among the players. The Shapley value solves this problem by trying out different coalitions of players to decide how much each player changes the amount of the payout. What does this have to do with machine learning? In machine learning, the features (= players) work together to get the payout (=predicted value). The Shapley value tells us, how much each feature contributed to the prediction.
We use Shapley value implementation in the R package DALEX.
crumbs: Comparison of Break Down, LIME and Shapley values

title: Comparison of Break Down, LIME and Shapley values
text:
Break Down
Break Down is the methodology delevoped by Przemysław Biecek and Mateusz Staniak. A description of the method can be found here.
This methodology is implemented by Przemysław Biecek and Mateusz Staniak in the R package breakDown. Currently available in the R package DALEX.
The breakDown package is a model agnostic tool for decomposition of predictions from black boxes. Break Down Table shows contributions of every variable to a final prediction. Break Down Profile presents variable contributions in a concise graphical way.
crumbs: Comparison of Break Down, LIME and Shapley values

title: Comparison of Break Down, LIME and Shapley values
text:
LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations)
LIME is the methodology developed by Marco Tulio Ribeiro, Sameer Singh, and Carlos Guestrin. A description of the method can be found here.
The purpose of LIME is to explain the predictions of black box classifiers. What this means is that for any given prediction and any given classifier it is able to determine a small set of features in the original data that has driven the outcome of the prediction. Using here package lime is an R port of the Python lime package (https://github.com/marcotcr/lime) developed by the authors of the lime approach for black-box model explanations.
crumbs: Comparison of Break Down, LIME and Shapley values

title: Comparison of Break Down, LIME and Shapley values
text:
Shapley value
A methodology based on the use of Shapley value known from game theory to explain predictions is developed by Scott Lundberg and Su-In Lee. A description of the method can be found here.
The Shapley value is a method that gives a solution to the following problem: A coalition of players play a game, for which they get a payout, but it is not clear how to distribute the payout fairly among the players. The Shapley value solves this problem by trying out different coalitions of players to decide how much each player changes the amount of the payout. What does this have to do with machine learning? In machine learning, the features (= players) work together to get the payout (=predicted value). The Shapley value tells us, how much each feature contributed to the prediction.
We use Shapley value implementation in the R package DALEX.
